title: After a Collapsed Bank and an Impeached President, What Lies Ahead for Paraguay?
text:
After a Collapsed Bank and an Impeached President, What Lies Ahead for Paraguay?

Photo: DANIEL DUARTE/AFP/Getty Images

Critical Questions
by

Juliana Rubio,

Henry Ziemer,
and
Olivia Licata

Published November 20, 2026

On November 5, Paraguay’s President Santiago Peña submitted his resignation to the nation’s Congress. The legislature, however, declined to accept this, and the following day elected instead to impeach the leader, who would find himself under arrest before the weekend was out. The proximate cause of this crisis in a country that had been assiduously cultivating a reputation for political stability was tied to the collapse of the Ueno Bank, one of Paraguay’s largest financial institutions, and although the immediate crisis appears to have passed, its full reverberations continue to play out.Q1: What caused Paraguay’s banking crisis, and what are its economic consequences?A1: The collapse of Ueno Bank is at the center of Paraguay’s current banking crisis. An investigation by the Paraguayan central bank revealed that Ueno Bank held under half of the capital necessary to meet the minimum solvency requirements, leading the central bank to take control of Ueno on Monday, November 2, 2026.Until this crisis, Paraguay had been gaining a global reputation as a strong economy and investment hub in Latin America. Paraguay has experienced an average annual GDP growth of 5.5 percent for three straight years, achieved an investment-grade sovereign credit rating every year since 2024, and maintained an annual inflation rate of 3.1 percent. Paraguay also has low public debt, composing just 38 percent of its GDP. These indicators reflect a generally healthy and growing economy.The rise of Ueno Bank coincided with this positive economic trend. Ueno Bank, a Paraguayan digital bank, began as a local fintech firm and grew to become a linchpin of the Paraguayan financial sector in just a few years. While its meteoric rise was once viewed as an impressive result of Paraguay’s regulatory openness and financial stability, the scandal revealed how the bank succumbed to clientelism, weak regulatory oversight, and questionable financial practices. Public funds, facilitated through President Santiago Peña, provided the bank with about $850 million in liquidity. These provided substantial capital and allowed the bank to provide low-interest loans to insider-owned companies, including companies that received government contracts. When regulatory institutions began investigating the bank’s operations following reports of noncompliance, they discovered its inadequate solvency.As a result of the collapse, Ueno Bank’s 3 million customers were unable to withdraw cash or use their credit cards. To mitigate the economic crisis, especially since one-third of the $2.8 billion in deposits is not expected to be returned, the government utilized its deposit guarantee fund. This fund provides up to $38,000 per person, which should cover about 97 percent of Ueno depositors. According to the central bank, 93 percent of eligible Ueno customers received a payment from the state by November 11, the legal deadline for it to provide advance payments. The remaining 7 percent of depositors either have restricted accounts, hold certificates of deposit, or do not have accounts with other institutions.The direct financial impact of the banking crisis is coupled with a significant loss of trust in financial and political institutions among Paraguayans. This distrust may discourage the population from using banks, reversing progress that the country made in recent years to expand access to credit and enroll people in formal financial institutions. Given that 60 percent of Paraguay’s adult population used Ueno Bank and one million customers were first-time bank users, the hit on morale is widespread throughout the country.Additionally, while the central bank emphasized that the wider financial system will not be impacted, credit rating agency Fitch has placed Paraguay’s sovereign credit rating on watch for a potential downgrade, financial institutions are strained under the burden of the deposit guarantee program, and local economies are experiencing a significant decline in business. Thus, skepticism will likely linger around the stability of the economy and capacity of institutions to govern the financial sector, impacting Paraguay’s long-term financial development and economic health.Q2: How was President Santiago Peña implicated in the banking scandal, what led to his impeachment, and what has happened since his removal from office?A2: Peña’s involvement in the Ueno scandal centers on allegations of conflicts of interest, regulatory manipulation, diverted pension funds, and personal financial benefit. In addition, according to prosecutors, he influenced the allocation of public funds to the bank, prevented regulators from intervening in the bank, and appointed Carlos Carvallo, a former Ueno executive, as the president of Paraguay’s central bank, the institution responsible for overseeing banks. There are still many questions to be answered, not only about Peña’s involvement, but also about other actors involved in what seems to be not only a regulatory failure but also a criminal scheme.The demise of Ueno Bank quickly became a political flashpoint. Peña lost support within his own party, and on November 5 submitted his resignation, which was rejected by Congress. Many argued that his resignation was an attempt to avoid the impeachment process and obtain the parliamentary immunity granted to former presidents who become senators for life under Paraguayan law. Very quickly, on November 6, the Senate voted to remove him, and Peña was arrested and placed in pretrial detention. Peña has denied wrongdoing. Meanwhile, Vice President Pedro Alliana assumed the presidency and is expected to complete the term until August 2028. Although the government acted quickly to leverage the deposit guarantee fund to reimburse the majority of eligible depositors, there are still hundreds of millions of dollars in public and pension funds that have not been recovered, and the larger question of where the money went remains unresolved.This crisis raises questions about Paraguay’s institutions and political accountability. The biggest question is why the institutions responsible for oversight failed to prevent the crisis in the first place. Some, like Paraguayan political analyst Esteban Caballero, point to other potential cases of wrongdoing that have not been fully investigated and question why the Prosecutor General delayed the execution of a search warrant. There have, in fact, been numerous allegations of corruption and clientelism during Peña’s administration, such as millions of dollars in public contracts awarded to a company previously linked to Peña, and contracts awarded through Itaipú, the country’s largest hydroelectric power plant, to the president’s political allies. Many of these allegations had received little institutional scrutiny during his presidency, with limited investigation or accountability, which does raise the question about the timing of the investigation.Alliana’s government now has to deal with the banking crisis, recover public funds, and restore confidence in the financial system. So far, he has replaced the leadership of the central bank, made changes to his cabinet, and pledged to support the investigations and generally return stability to the country. Caballero argues that among the immediate priorities are restoring the autonomy of the central bank, recovering public funds, and genuinely allowing investigations to move forward. Perhaps the bigger question is whether these investigations will actually reach the broader network of political and financial actors involved, or whether accountability will be limited to Peña and a few others.Q3: What are the politics behind Paraguay’s banking scandal, and what could it mean for the country’s political landscape?A3: The crisis facing Paraguay also has political roots and implications. President Peña’s rise to power was enabled by the highly influential—and equally controversial—businessman and political figure Horacio Cartes. Cartes was president of Paraguay from 2013 to 2018, but his true power stems from his enormous fortune and network of influence among Paraguay’s elite, media, and the Colorado Party. His influence is disproportionate in Paraguayan politics, given that the Colorado Party has won every presidential election since Paraguay began its transition to democracy in 1989, bar the 2008 victory of opposition candidate Fernando Lugo.While much of the Colorado Party, particularly the faction led by Cartes, “Honor Colorado,” turned its back on Peña because of the Ueno crisis, friction had already emerged earlier this year. Peña’s vice president, Pedro Alliana, whom Cartes had backed as the candidate for the party in the 2028 presidential election, didn’t support Cartes’s pick for vice president, saying it was too early to decide. Peña backed Alliana, thereby also defying Cartes’s choice. Separately, Peña had also been promoting Marco Riquelme as a potential presidential candidate, a move interpreted as an attempt to maintain influence beyond his presidency. Interestingly, senators aligned with Cartes had started to raise questions about Ueno’s operations and regulatory oversight in September 2026, and the eventual collapse of the bank gave Cartes an opportunity to distance himself from Peña and weaken his political ambitions, while also reasserting his influence within the party.Peña’s removal from office doesn’t mean that the Colorado Party has been removed from power. In fact, some have argued that Peña’s removal was a “controlled implosion” to preserve the Colorado Party’s hold on power. While the crisis has affected public trust, it is still unclear whether most Paraguayans will blame the party and begin turning their backs on it, or whether efforts to distance the party from Peña, particularly by Honor Colorado and Cartes, will be enough to continue giving the party the upper hand in future elections. It also remains to be seen who Cartes will back for the 2028 presidential election, as Alliana, now president, cannot seek reelection under Paraguay’s Constitution. Another question is whether Alliana will retreat from his previous defiance of Cartes, perhaps seeing Peña’s downfall as a warning of the cost of such disobedience.For the opposition, the crisis could create an opening, but so far, it does not seem to be “reading the historical moment” or seizing the opportunity to form an organized coalition; internal disputes and individual political ambitions continue to prevent cohesion. The question is then whether the opposition can capitalize on the crisis. The important victory of Soledad Núñez in Asunción during the municipal elections held on October 4 could position the opposition to become a credible national alternative and raises questions about whether the now-battered Colorado Party can once again overcome its divisions and maintain power. More fundamentally, Peña’s removal raises the question of whether institutional reforms will actually be implemented, or whether the crisis will lead only to political reshuffling within the same party.Q4: What are the international implications of the situation in Paraguay?A4: Paraguay has sought to market itself as a stable and attractive destination for foreign businesses. In recent years the country’s low taxes, including no tax on income earned abroad, openness to foreigners, and cheap and abundant hydroelectricity have made it a particularly desirable South American haven for first cryptocurrency investors, and more recently data center developers. Meanwhile, steady progress in the country’s agricultural and service sectors helped Paraguay become one of the fastest-growing economies in South America, although the Ueno crisis has raised questions about the country’s economic stability. Beyond the economic domain, President Peña also sought to position himself as an important ally of the United States in South America, joining the Shield of the Americas grouping as well as signing a Status of Forces Agreement facilitating the temporary deployment of U.S. military personnel “to deepen and strengthen the security relationship” between the two countries.For the time being, the crisis in Paraguay is unlikely to dramatically impact Paraguay’s foreign policy outlook. President Alliana is likely to have enough on his hands wrangling his cabinet and Congress, as well as managing the economic fallout from Ueno’s collapse. Still, Paraguay is likely to turn to its allies, especially the United States, for help in restoring its reputation as a stable and attractive investment destination. Early signs also point to the new president continuing his former boss’s alignment with the United States on security issues in the hemisphere, as Alliana recently issued a spate of terrorist designations for Western Hemisphere–based criminal groups including the Tren de Aragua, Gulf Cartel, and National Liberation Army. However, if the United States is seen as failing to provide vital support in a time of need, it could not only weaken the new Alliana government but potentially prompt some within Paraguay to question whether close relations with the Trump administration are worthwhile.Another key partner to watch will be Taiwan. Because it is the only country in South America that diplomatically recognizes Taiwan in lieu of the People’s Republic of China, domestic developments in Paraguay can carry outsized geopolitical relevance. China has consistently sought to flip the country’s diplomatic allegiances as it has elsewhere in the region, including by sponsoring trips by opposition lawmakers to China. While at present there are no signs that the impeachment scandal will immediately jeopardize Taiwan’s status as a key partner for Paraguay, it underscores the importance of cultivating support for continued recognition across the political spectrum.Indeed, Paraguay’s diplomatic allegiances are liable to become a significant point of debate as presidential elections in the country approach in 2028. By continuing to press forward with key investments, such as a planned $200 million data center project supported by Taiwan’s International Cooperation and Development Fund and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, Taipei and Washington can provide an important vote of confidence in the Paraguayan economy. Still, the present scandal has underscored structural impediments to growth stemming from transparency and governance gaps that Paraguay’s allies should encourage it to resolve.Juliana Rubio is associate director and associate fellow in the Americas Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) in Washington, D.C. Henry Ziemer is a fellow in the Americas Program at CSIS. Olivia Licata is an intern in the Americas Program at CSIS.
